KEY MESSAGE 1...
Well above normal temperatures will continue today along with 
increased dew points keeping heat indices in the upper 90s to low 
100s. The upper level ridge continues to be in place across the 
southern CONUS allowing for persistent west to southwesterly flow 
across the region to continue today into the overnight. This will 
push highs today a touch warmer into the low 90s with dew points 
climbing into the low to mid 70s again. Heat indices as a result 
will rise up into the upper 90s to low 100s. Portions of Western 
Ohio will be warmer than to the east as there should be limited 
precipitation and cloud cover for much of the day. For Cleveland 
eastward, precipitation is expected this morning and again in the 
evening, but there should be a long enough break in between to allow 
for temperatures to climb quickly. For the Northwestern Pennsylvania 
areas, they will be far enough east to were temperatures shouldn't 
climb up into the 90s, therefore heat indices will be below advisory 
criteria. With that being said, it still will feel hot with heat 
indices in the mid 90s, and precautions should be taken as needed. 
Overnight lows Wednesday into Thursday will still be elevated as 
well into the low to mid 70s offering little relief. Heat risk will 
stay elevated at a level 3 out of 4 for the entire CWA due to this. 

Thursday will start to bring some relief to the region as a cold 
front approaches from the north and more widespread precipitation is 
expected at some point during the day. Western and Central Ohio will 
still have elevated heat indices and heat risk though, as 
precipitation will not have reached before peak heating. There is 
some uncertainty in this as morning convection may be moving across 
the area that would limit the high temperatures for the day. If the 
convection does not pan out, then thinking is that an area from 
roughly Wayne/Holmes northwest to Lucas will need an extension in 
the advisory. The remainder of the eastern portions of the CWA 
should have enough precipitation and cloud cover to keep 
temperatures and heat indices down in the upper 80s and low to mid 
90s respectively. 

Temperatures will begin to regulate Friday into the weekend to more 
seasonal as Canadian high pressure builds south into the region. 
Highs will be in the upper 70s to mid 80s with overnight lows in the 
upper 50s to mid 60s through the weekend. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
More rounds of showers and thunderstorms are expected this morning 
through the overnight hours. For this morning, there is a shortwave 
trough located over Southern Ontario that will push southeastward 
into New York through the mid-morning. This will help support 
scattered showers and thunderstorms this morning across Northeastern 
Ohio and Northwestern Pennsylvania. There will be some instability 
in place along with around 40 knots of bulk shear that, if storms 
organize, could support damaging wind gusts. Will monitor upstream 
in Southern Ontario and Eastern Michigan for storm formation, but 
currently storms across Western Michigan have started to weaken and 
the environment may not be suitable for thunderstorm development. 

There will be a break in the showers and precipitation once the 
shortwave moves eastward and the next shortwave enters the region 
later this afternoon/evening. This will allow for instability to 
build back to around 2000 J/kg and lapse rates of 7-7.5 C/km across 
Eastern Ohio and Northwestern Pennsylvania. Bulk shear will also in 
the neighborhood of 30-40 knots in that same region. Thunderstorm 
development is possible ahead of the shortwave with a more linear 
mode expected with the shortwave later in the evening. The western 
extent of this feature is still uncertain and could reach as far 
west as Cleveland. The highest confidence in thunderstorms currently 
for this evening is across far Northeastern Ohio and in Northwestern 
Pennsylvania. This is shown in SPC's Day 1 Severe Weather Outlook as 
there is a slight risk (level 3 of 5) from a line from Toledo 
southeast to Canton and eastward with higher probabilities for 
severe winds in Northeastern Ohio and Northwestern Pennsylvania. 
Damaging winds will be the main threat with todays storms, though 
large hail will also be a factor with the increased lapse rates and 
instability. A quick spin up tornado is also possible though 0-1 km 
bulk shear is minimal, so the threat is on the low end. 
Thunderstorms should exit to the southeast around midnight.
Given the warm, moist environment over the region, PWAT values 
will be around 1.5-2.00" across the region. The will bring the 
threat for heavy rain with any thunderstorms and could cause 
isolated flooding issues if there are persistent rainfall over 
and area.
